claim: Stem shrinkage turned into a daily irrigation traffic light caught 38 of 38 simulated droughts.
data_label: simulated orchard seasons (real Visp weather) | open data: EnviDat Pfynwald pines 2024-2025, MeteoSwiss
limit: Real data are forest pines, not orchards; no own sensors; thresholds not calibrated per species.
alt: Line chart of predawn tree water deficit at dawn for Scots pines in Valais from April to September 2025: rain-only trees climb highest, roof-covered trees next, irrigated trees stay lowest, with rain bars below and summary numbers.
post:
An orchard can be short of water days before the leaves show it, and soil probes only see one spot of the root zone. A point dendrometer on the trunk sees the tree itself: every afternoon the stem shrinks a few tens of micrometres and refills at night.

I built an open-source tool that turns those 10-minute readings into a daily traffic light. It cleans sensor faults, computes maximum daily shrinkage, growth and tree water deficit, and compares the shrink with well-watered reference trees or with an air-dryness baseline.

On 20 simulated orchard seasons driven by real Valais weather, it flagged all 38 injected droughts, at most 2 days after the soil became limiting, with 8.6% of well-watered days falsely flagged. On open data from 72 Scots pines in an irrigation experiment, rain-fed trees were flagged on 77% of summer 2025 days and irrigated trees on 42%. Injected jumps and resets in the real series were found 119 of 120 times.

What is not verified: the real trees are forest pines, not fruit trees; I have no own sensors; the thresholds are not calibrated per species, and the irrigated pines still got too many alarms.

If you irrigate by sensor, would you trust the trunk or the soil probe more?

Code: https://github.com/VB-Builds/dendrometer-stress-index
